c.tagline: Japan's most storied hot-spring town, steaming beside the Yubatake

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are clean, safe, and expensive by distance; most visitors get around on foot or by the town's onsen loop bus instead.

emergency.note: 119 covers both ambulance and fire; some English support is available on emergency lines in this tourist area.

hood_desc: The steaming, sulfur-scented heart of town, built around the wooden troughs of the Yubatake where hot spring water cascades and glows at night; ryokan, shops, and foot baths ring the square.
A wooded park a short walk uphill from the center, with free open-air baths tucked among the trees and a peaceful, forested atmosphere away from the main crowds.
A quieter residential onsen district with small local bathhouses used more by residents than tourists, offering an everyday, unpolished side of the town.
The main shopping street lined with souvenir shops, izakaya, and the Netsu-no-Yu bathhouse, where staff perform the traditional 'yumomi' water-cooling dance.
The edge of town where the road climbs toward Mt. Kusatsu-Shirane's volcanic crater lake, popular for hiking and ropeway views in warmer months.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink; hot-spring water is for bathing only.

transit.pay: cash or IC card on board
transit.map: available at the tourist information center near the Yubatake
transit.note: The town center is compact and walkable; the loop bus mainly helps reach outlying ryokan and the ropeway.

air: No local airport; nearest is Tokyo Haneda (HND)
train: JR Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi Station, then a 25-minute connecting bus into town
bus: Direct highway buses run from Tokyo (Shinjuku/Ikebukuro), about 4 hours

tip.r: Tipping is not practiced and can cause confusion; excellent service is simply the norm, included in the price.
